newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian president names caretaker cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian president names caretaker cabinet.

text.p: Bulgarian President Petar Stoyanov on Wednesday named an interim cabinet led by Sofia's respected mayor Stefan Sofianski to govern until after elections in mid-April, the presidency said.
After 30 days of mass protests, the Socialists last week gave up efforts to form a new cabinet and agreed to elections in April, 20 months before the end of their parliamentary term.
The cabinet contains several critics of the outgoing Socialist government, and abolishes the economic development portfolio created by the Socialists.
Bulgaria's ambassador to Bonn, Stoyan Stalev, will be foreign minister, and the deputy finance minister from the outgoing government, Svetoslav Gavriiski, will be finance minister.
Alexander Bozhkov, deputy leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces and a former director of Bulgaria's Privatisation Agency, will be deputy prime minister and minister of industry.
The health ministry will be headed by Emil Takov, a senior doctor and one of the leaders of protests at Pirogov emergency hospital against the current Socialist health administration.

The rector of Sofia university, Ivan Lalov, is named education minister, while the trade ministry will be headed by Daniela Bobeva, who resigned from the foreign investment agency last year saying changes to the foreign investment law did not go far enough.
"I hope that the caretaker cabinet will win back confidence in the administration," Sofianski said.

The interim cabinet will take office once parliament has cleared outstanding business. Sofianski said the customary ceremonial handover, where the incoming and outgoing administrations drink champagne together, would not take place.
Parliament met on Wednesday to discuss changes to the electoral law and a bill authorising the interim cabinet to negotiate vital loans.
Deputies are expected to complete the eight-item agenda on Thursday, and Stoyanov will then dissolve the assembly.

Authorising the caretaker cabinet to negotiate with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will pave the way for talks on new aid to accompany a strict fixed exchange rate regime to shore up the collapsing economy.
After initial resistance, the majority Socialists agreed on Tuesday to support the move.

"We have tried to convince our colleagues to support the expansion of the powers of the interim government. We hope they will support it for the common good of Bulgaria," Socialist deputy Nikola Koichev, head of parliament's budget committee, told Reuters.
On Tuesday, leaders of the five parties in parliament signed a "Declaration on the Principles of Emergence from the Crisis", saying it showed unprecedented political consensus.

They agreed the caretaker cabinet must speed up long-delayed structural reforms such as privatisation and closing loss-making state firms, cutting state spending, cracking down on corruption and the grey economy, and encouraging investment.
The IMF has said it is ready to send a mission to Sofia as soon as a new government is in place, and Stoyanov has asked for aid to stabilise the economy before introduction of a currency board.
The currency board mechanism requires levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely limiting the powers of the government and the central bank.
Central bank governor Lyubomir Filipov said on Tuesday that it could be introduced in June.
